Title: The effectiveness evaluation of industry education integration model for applied universities under back propagation neural network

The effectiveness evaluation of 
industry education integration 
model for applied universities 
under back propagation neural 
network
Ying Qi1,2 & Wei Feng3
As the education field continues to advance, industry–education integration has become a crucial 
strategy for enhancing teaching quality in applied universities. This study investigates how artificial 
intelligence, specifically the back propagation neural network (BPNN), can be applied within an 
industry–education integration framework to strengthen students’ skills and employability. A series 
of experiments were conducted to assess the model’s effectiveness in linking theoretical learning 
with practical experience, as well as in improving students’ hands-on and innovative abilities. Results 
demonstrate that the BPNN-optimized model substantially boosts students’ overall competencies. 
For instance, the average academic score of students in the experimental group rose from 78.5 to 85.2, 
practical assessment scores increased from 76.8 to 88.4, and innovation scores improved from 74.2 
to 82.5. Additionally, the employment rate for the experimental group reached 94%, surpassing the 
control group’s 76%, with significant gains in job satisfaction and career planning skills. These findings 
highlight that the BPNN-based industry–education integration model effectively strengthens students’ 
theoretical knowledge, practical skills, and employability, offering a valuable framework for enhanced 
university-industry collaboration.
Keywords  BPNN, Industry–education integration, Applied universities, Teaching quality, Employability
Research background and motivations
With the rapid growth of the global economy and ongoing technological advancements, there is an escalating 
demand for highly skilled applied professionals. Applied universities, which play a vital role in cultivating 
such talent, are tasked with enhancing teaching quality, improving students’ practical skills, and boosting their 
employability1–3. However, conventional teaching methods often prioritize theoretical knowledge while failing 
to effectively integrate practical application, leading to gaps in students’ hands-on and innovative capabilities. As 
a result, developing a teaching model that bridges theory and practice has become increasingly crucial.
Emerging technologies such as big data, cloud computing, and the Internet of Things have paved the way for 
artificial intelligence (AI) to drive industrial and societal progress4,5. Li et al.6 highlighted AI’s role in helping 
companies reduce costs and revolutionize innovative tools in the digital age. Among AI algorithms, the back 
propagation neural network (BPNN) stands out for its robust data processing abilities and high predictive 
accuracy. It has demonstrated impressive results in areas like image recognition, natural language processing, and 
financial forecasting. By emulating the workings of human neurons, BPNN can automatically learn from large 
datasets and tackle complex tasks, making it especially effective for solving real-world challenges, particularly 
those involving nonlinear, uncertain, and multivariable problems7–9.
This study seeks to enhance the industry–education integration model by integrating AI technology, 
specifically leveraging the capabilities of BPNN, to advance teaching quality and students’ comprehensive 
skill sets within applied universities. BPNN, known for its robust data processing and predictive strengths, is 
used to analyze and extract insights from multidimensional student data, supporting personalized education 
approaches and offering targeted guidance based on individual learning profiles. By designing and conducting

Research objectives
This study aims to optimize the industry–education integration model by introducing AI technology based on 
BPNN, with specific objectives including: (1) enhancing students’ theoretical academic performance and practical 
abilities; (2) improving students’ innovation and career planning skills; (3) increasing students’ employment rate 
and job satisfaction; and (4) providing new ideas and methods for in-depth collaboration between universities 
and enterprises. Through achieving these objectives, this study aims to provide robust support for improving the 
teaching quality of applied universities and fostering the development of students’ comprehensive skills.
The innovations of this study are as follows:
•	 By combining BPNN technology with the industry–education integration model, this study proposes a cus­
tomized BPNN model tailored to the characteristics of applied higher education. It offers a new theoretical 
perspective and practical pathway for the field of education.
•	 Through the comprehensive analysis of multidimensional student data, this study innovatively enhances the 
prediction accuracy and practicality of the BPNN model, providing a more holistic view of students’ ability 
development and employment potential.
•	 This study conducts a comprehensive evaluation of the BPNN industry–education integration model in terms 
of its impact on improving students’ academic performance, practical skills, innovative abilities, and employ­
ment competitiveness, offering empirical support for validating the model’s effectiveness.
•	 This study provides a strategic framework for the reform of applied higher education by strengthening uni­
versity-industry collaboration, driving educational reform, and meeting the demand for highly skilled, appli­
cation-oriented talent in society and industry.
Literature review
Application of BPNN in the education field
In recent years, the application of BPNN in education has grown, particularly in areas such as personalized 
learning, student performance prediction, and educational resource optimization10–12. In personalized learning 
recommendations, Smirani et al.13 proposed a BPNN-based personalized learning recommendation system, 
which suggested the most suitable courses and learning resources for students based on their learning behaviors 
and academic data. Experimental results demonstrated that the system significantly improved students’ learning 
efficiency and satisfaction13.
In student performance prediction, Olabanjo et al.14 utilized BPNN to predict students’ final exam scores. 
The findings indicated that BPNN could accurately predict student performance, enabling timely intervention by 
instructors to improve teaching effectiveness14. In educational resource optimization, Sun and Zhang15 explored 
BPNN’s application in optimizing educational resources. They developed a BPNN-based resource allocation 
system that dynamically adjusted resource distribution according to students’ needs and resource availability, 
thereby enhancing resource utilization efficiency15.
The concept of industry–education integration and analysis of existing models
Industry–education integration refers to the close cooperation between education and industry through school-
enterprise collaboration, integration of production, teaching, and research, and other methods to achieve 
resource sharing and complementary strengths, thereby cultivating high-quality talent that meets market 
demand. In recent years, industry–education integration has become a key direction for educational reform in 
applied universities16. In terms of school-enterprise cooperation models, He and Sun17 conducted a systematic 
analysis of school-enterprise cooperation models domestically and internationally, pointing out that successful 
cooperation required clarifying the responsibilities and benefits of both parties and establishing long-term, 
stable partnerships. They proposed a project-driven school-enterprise cooperation model, in which students 
participated in real-world projects within enterprises, thereby enhancing their practical and innovative abilities17. 
Regarding the integration of production, teaching, and research, Ravi and Janodia18 studied its application 
in applied universities. By establishing research platforms and technology transfer centers, universities and 
enterprises could jointly conduct technological research and innovation, not only enhancing students’ research 
capabilities but also promoting the commercialization of technological achievements18.
In terms of virtual simulation experiments, Elfakki et al.19 explored the role of virtual simulation experiments 
in industry–education integration. They developed a virtual reality-based experimental platform that allowed 
students to perform various experimental operations in a virtual environment, addressing the issue of limited 
practical experimental resources. Virtual simulation experiments could significantly enhance students’ interest 
in learning and their practical abilities19.
Research on BPNN-based industry–education integration model
Although BPNN has achieved some successes in the field of education, its application in the industry–education 
integration model is still in the early stages. In the area of intelligent course recommendation systems, Liu et 
al.20 designed a BPNN-based intelligent course recommendation system capable of suggesting the most suitable 
courses for students based on their learning history and interest preferences. The experimental results showed

In summary, existing research has demonstrated the broad potential of BPNN in the field of education, 
especially in areas such as personalized learning recommendations, student performance prediction, and 
educational resource optimization. However, research that combines BPNN technology with the industry–
education integration model remains in its early stages, with research gaps in multimodal data fusion, dynamic 
adjustment mechanisms, and interdisciplinary collaboration. Therefore, this study aims to design and implement 
a BPNN-based industry–education integration model, further exploring its application effectiveness in applied 
universities and providing new ideas and methods for future educational reform.
Research model
Selection and construction of the BPNN model
BPNN
Basic principles of BPNN: The BPNN is a multilayer feedforward neural network trained using the 
backpropagation algorithm. It is widely used in fields such as pattern recognition, classification, and regression23.
The basic structure of the BPNN includes an input layer, hidden layers, and an output layer, with weights 
connecting each layer. During training, the network first performs a forward pass of input data to calculate the 
output. Then, based on the output error, it adjusts the weights in a backward direction, gradually minimizing 
the error until it meets a predefined convergence condition24. The core of the BPNN lies in its backpropagation 
algorithm, which updates weights using the gradient descent method. The specific steps are as follows:
First is forward propagation, where input data flows from the input layer to the output layer. The output of 
each neuron in a layer is calculated by taking a weighted sum of the previous layer’s outputs and applying an 
activation function. Letting zl

In Fig. 1, the specific application of the BPNN is as follows:
First, the input layer is designed to include multiple features related to student performance and engagement, 
such as academic achievements, participation in practical activities, and internship feedback. These features are 
selected based on their potential to influence student outcomes and are normalized to ensure consistency in the 
input layer.
Second, the BPNN utilizes a dual-path architecture with two hidden layers to handle the complexity of 
predicting educational outcomes. This configuration enables the model to capture both linear and nonlinear 
relationships in the data, enhancing its ability to learn and generalize patterns observed in student data. The two 
hidden layers provide additional capacity for processing the complex interactions between input features, which 
is crucial for accurately modeling the multifaceted nature of student performance.
Third, the weight initialization and optimization process (w1–w4) in this study is crucial to the model’s 
performance. Weights are initialized using a random normal distribution to break symmetry and encourage 
diverse feature learning during the early stages of training. The optimization process employs the Adam

Fourth, the size of the hidden layers is determined through a series of hyperparameter tuning experiments. 
The first hidden layer contains 128 nodes, and the second hidden layer contains 64 nodes. This configuration 
strikes a balance between the model’s ability to learn complex patterns and the risk of overfitting. The number of 
nodes in each layer is chosen to ensure the model has sufficient representational capacity while maintaining its 
ability to generalize to new data. In the context of educational applications, this balance is essential for achieving 
high predictive accuracy and robustness.
Selection and construction of the BPNN model
In this study, the BPNN was chosen as the core model for its ability to efficiently process data and deliver high 
levels of prediction accuracy. To enhance both the model’s performance and its stability, multiple critical aspects 
were considered throughout the model’s design and implementation stages.
Firstly, the network structure was carefully designed, comprising an input layer, hidden layers, and an output 
layer. The number of nodes in the input layer was set according to the number of input features, while the 
output layer nodes corresponded to the number of target outputs. The configuration of hidden layers, including 
the number of layers and nodes in each layer, was optimized through experimentation. Generally, adding 
more hidden layers or nodes can increase the model’s representational power, though it may also introduce a 
risk of overfitting if not carefully managed. Fine-tuning this balance is essential for achieving optimal model 
performance.
Secondly, the selection of the activation function significantly influences the model’s accuracy and 
computational efficiency. Common activation functions such as Sigmoid, ReLU, and Tanh each have distinct 
characteristics. For this study, ReLU was employed in the hidden layers due to its ability to prevent the vanishing 
gradient problem and improve convergence speed. For the output layer, different activation functions were 
selected based on the task requirements: Softmax was applied for classification, while a linear activation function 
was used for regression tasks. This task-specific choice of activation functions helps to ensure the network is 
well-suited for the problem at hand and can yield reliable predictions25.
Thirdly, the loss function, which quantifies the error between predicted and actual values, is another pivotal 
component of the BPNN. The choice of loss function directly impacts how the model learns during training. 
In this study, mean squared error (MSE) was chosen as the loss function due to its suitability for regression-
based tasks, as outlined in Eq.  (7). MSE effectively penalizes larger errors more heavily, which aids in the 
accurate refinement of model parameters to minimize prediction errors. Other potential loss functions, such as 
cross-entropy for classification tasks, were considered based on the task type but ultimately not selected in this 
regression-focused context26.
By carefully addressing each of these factors—network structure, activation function, and loss function—the 
BPNN model was designed to provide robust and stable performance, ensuring it meets the study’s objectives 
effectively. This thorough configuration of the model’s architecture strengthens its capacity to generalize well 
on unseen data and reinforces its utility in educational applications where accurate predictions and responsive 
feedback are critical.

The fourth key factor is the optimization algorithm, which is used to update the network weights27,28. 
Common optimization algorithms include gradient descent, momentum, and Adam. In this study, the Adam 
optimization algorithm is selected due to its combination of the benefits of momentum and RMSprop, enabling 
faster convergence while minimizing the risk of getting stuck in local optima.
Specific implementation methods of the industry–education integration model
	(1)	 Intelligent course recommendation system.
The intelligent course recommendation system is an essential part of the industry–education integration 
model based on BPNN. This system analyzes multidimensional data, such as students’ learning history, interest 
preferences, and performance records, to provide personalized course recommendations for each student.
	(2)	 Employment guidance services.
Employment guidance services are a key component of the BPNN-based industry–education integration model, 
aimed at helping students better plan their career paths and improve their competitiveness in the job market. The 
specific implementation steps are as follows:
First, data preprocessing is performed by collecting students’ learning history data, including course 
selection records, grades, learning behaviors, etc. The data is then cleaned and standardized to ensure quality and 
consistency. Second, feature extraction involves extracting useful features from the preprocessed data, such as 
students’ learning interests, learning abilities, and course difficulties. This process is carried out using statistical 
analysis and machine learning methods. Third, model training is conducted using BPNN to train the extracted

features and construct the course recommendation model. The model’s input is the student’s feature vector, 
and the output is the probability distribution of recommended courses. During training, mean squared error is 
used as the loss function, and the Adam optimization algorithm is applied for weight updates. Fourth, service 
provision involves offering students personalized career planning advice and job search guidance based on the 
model’s output. The advice and guidance include career directions, skill training, interview techniques, etc. Fifth, 
effect evaluation is carried out through user surveys and experimental data to assess the effectiveness of the 
employment guidance services. Key indicators include student employment rates, job satisfaction, and career 
development.
	(3)	 School-enterprise cooperation mechanism.
The school-enterprise cooperation mechanism is a core element of the industry–education integration model29, 
aiming to promote deep communication and cooperation between universities and enterprises, achieving 
resource sharing and complementary advantages. The specific implementation steps are as follows:
First, platform construction involves establishing a web-based school-enterprise cooperation platform that 
provides functions such as information release, project management, and resource matching. The platform uses 
a modular design for easy expansion and maintenance. Second, project cooperation encourages enterprises to 
play an active role in course design, training base construction, and teacher training, ensuring that the teaching 
content aligns closely with industry demands. Enterprises can use the platform to post project requirements 
and invite university staff and students to participate in real-world projects. Third, resource matching is 
implemented through the platform, facilitating resource connections between universities and enterprises, such 
as experimental equipment, training bases, and research projects. Resource matching helps improve teaching 
quality and students’ practical abilities. Fourth, effect evaluation is conducted through experimental data and 
user feedback to assess the effectiveness of the school-enterprise cooperation mechanism. Key indicators include 
project completion quality, students’ practical skills, and enterprise satisfaction.
The flowchart of the BPNN-based industry–education integration model is shown in Fig. 2.
Figure 2 illustrates the logical framework of the BPNN-based industry–education integration model. First, 
the specific implementation of BPNN in each component is as follows. In the intelligent course recommendation 
system, the BPNN analyzes multidimensional data such as students’ academic performance, interest preferences, 
and past course records to provide personalized course suggestions. In the career guidance service, the BPNN 
uses students’ learning history and abilities to offer career planning advice and an analysis of their competitiveness 
in the job market. In the school-enterprise cooperation mechanism, the BPNN helps match enterprise needs 
with student capabilities, fostering project collaboration and resource sharing. The preprocessing methods for 
different types of input data include data cleaning, feature extraction, and normalization. Data cleaning aims to 
remove missing and outlier values, ensuring the quality and consistency of the data. Feature extraction involves 
extracting key information from the raw data that contributes to model training, such as students’ learning habits, 
grade trends, and social interactions. Normalization processes scale all feature data to a common range, enabling 
the model to learn more effectively. These preprocessing steps are crucial for enhancing the performance and 
accuracy of the BPNN model.
Second, the data flow between the course recommendation, career guidance, and enterprise cooperation 
systems is bidirectional and dynamically adjusted. Students’ personal information and academic performance 
data flow from the school management system into the BPNN model, which processes this data to provide 
course recommendations and career development advice. Additionally, student feedback and enterprise needs 
are updated back into the model to continually optimize the recommendation algorithms and collaboration 
projects. The exact role of BPNN in each decision-making step lies in its ability to automatically learn and 
adjust based on the input feature data to predict the best course matches, career paths, and collaboration 
opportunities. This predictive capability enables BPNN to independently support decision-making without 
explicit programming instructions, offering more precise services for students and enterprises.
Experimental design and performance evaluation
Datasets collection
This study collects student data from an applied university in S Province between February 1, 2023, and January 
30, 2024, to comprehensively evaluate the effectiveness of the BPNN-based industry–education integration 
model. The data sources include multiple dimensions such as students’ basic information, academic performance, 
internship performance, practical activities, and career development. Specifically, the students’ basic information 
includes gender, age, hometown, family background, college entrance examination scores, admitted majors, 
and enrollment dates; academic performance includes course grades for each semester, midterm exams, final 
exams, and scores from various certification exams; internship performance records the internship projects 
students participated in, internship organizations, internship duration, internship positions, and the evaluations 
provided by the internship organizations; practical activities include both on-campus and off-campus projects, 
competitions, and industry collaboration projects, as well as the awards received in various competitions; career 
development data records students’ employment destinations, employers, positions, salaries, and career planning 
information.
The experiment carefully selected 300 students as research subjects to ensure the representativeness and validity 
of the sample. This sample size was determined based on power analysis, a statistical method used to estimate the 
minimum sample size required to detect a given effect size. A sample size of 300 was chosen to provide a 95% 
confidence level, ensuring its validity. After selecting the subjects, they were randomly assigned to the experimental 
group (A) and the control group (B), with 150 participants in each group. The randomization process was carried 
out using a computer-generated random number list, ensuring that each student had an equal probability of being

environments. All participants provided written informed consent, and the study was reviewed and approved by 
the ethics committees of the participating universities, ensuring the ethical integrity of the study and the protection 
of participants’ rights.

Experimental environment
To ensure the reliability and reproducibility of the results, the experiments were conducted under a strict software 
and hardware environment. The experimental environment includes high-performance computing servers, 
specialized data processing software, and secure data storage systems. Specifically, in terms of hardware, a high-
performance computing server equipped with an Intel Xeon E5-2690 v4 processor, 128GB DDR4 memory, and 
an NVIDIA Tesla P100 GPU was used to ensure efficient large-scale data processing and model training. On the 
software side, the Python 3.8 programming language, along with TensorFlow 2.4 and Keras 2.4 deep learning 
frameworks, was employed to build and train the BPNN model. Additionally, the Pandas and NumPy libraries were 
used for data preprocessing and analysis, while Matplotlib and Seaborn libraries were used for visual presentations. 
In terms of data storage, the MySQL database management system was used to ensure the security and integrity 
of the data. The entire experimental environment is connected via a local area network (LAN) to ensure fast and 
stable data transmission. These software and hardware configurations enable efficient and accurate data processing, 
model training, and result evaluation, providing solid technical support for the smooth progress of the study.
Parameters setting
In the training process of the BPNN model, setting key parameters reasonably is crucial for the model’s performance 
and stability. This study carefully set the following key parameters to ensure efficient training and good performance 
of the model. First, the learning rate η was set to 0.001, which was determined to be the optimal value through grid 
search and random search methods, balancing the model’s convergence speed and stability. Second, the number 
of hidden layers was set to 2, with 128 nodes in the first layer and 64 nodes in the second layer. This structure 
was determined through cross-validation, capturing the complex features of the data while avoiding overfitting. 
Third, the regularization parameter λ was set to 0.0001, and L2 regularization was applied to effectively prevent 
overfitting. Fourth, the batch size was set to 32, providing enough sample diversity while ensuring training speed, 
which improves the model’s generalization ability. Fifth, the number of epochs was set to 100, and early stopping 
was used to monitor the performance on the validation set. If the error on the validation set no longer decreased, 
training was terminated early to prevent overtraining.

	(4)	 Employment rate.
The employment rate of both groups of students was analyzed (Fig. 6).

salary for the experimental group was 6500 RMB, compared to 5800 RMB for the control group, reflecting better

stable than the control group’s (4500–7500 RMB), further highlighting the higher and more stable employment 
quality of the experimental group.

The employment satisfaction of both groups of students was analyzed (Fig. 7).
The experimental group students had significantly higher and more stable employment satisfaction than 
the control group, as indicated by a smaller standard deviation. The smaller gap between the highest and lowest 
scores further suggests more balanced satisfaction among the experimental group.

The career planning ability of both groups of students was analyzed (Fig. 8).

innovation. Employment rate statistics show that the experimental group has a significantly higher employment 
rate than the control group, and the average monthly salary and salary range also indicate that the experimental 
group enjoys higher employment quality. In terms of job satisfaction, the experimental group exhibits higher 
satisfaction and a smaller standard deviation, demonstrating greater stability and balance in employment 
satisfaction. Career planning ability analysis also shows that the experimental group’s career planning ability is 
significantly higher than that of the control group, with a more concentrated ability distribution. Finally, user 
satisfaction analysis reveals that the experimental group’s satisfaction with the industry–education integration 
model is significantly higher than that of the control group, with a more balanced satisfaction distribution. These 
statistical differences (*p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001) indicate that the BPNN-optimized industry–education 
integration model significantly enhances students’ overall capabilities and employment competitiveness across 
multiple dimensions.
Discussion
This study conducted a comprehensive evaluation of students’ various abilities using the BPNN-based industry–
education integration model. The results revealed that students in the experimental group significantly 
outperformed those in the control group in several areas, including academic performance, practical skills, 
innovation ability, employment rate, job satisfaction, career planning ability, and user satisfaction. These 
findings are consistent with existing literature. When comparing the results of this study with existing methods 
in the literature, the findings align with those of Zhang and Wang30, who demonstrated similar significant 
improvements in student academic performance using a BPNN model. This not only further validates the

model. Furthermore, the study by Hou et al.31 emphasized the effectiveness of virtual simulation experiments 
and project-driven practice platforms in enhancing students’ practical and innovative abilities. This conclusion 
is consistent with the findings of the present study, suggesting that the BPNN model can effectively improve 
students’ practical skills and innovation capabilities. In terms of employment rate and satisfaction, Deng 
et al.32 demonstrated the significant impact of BPNN-based career guidance services in improving students’ 
employment rates and satisfaction, further confirming the advantage of the BPNN model in enhancing students’ 
employment competitiveness. These comparisons indicate that the BPNN-based industry–education integration 
model is competitive in several key areas and has practical application value in enhancing students’ overall 
capabilities and employment prospects.
While this study achieved positive results in the implementation of the BPNN-based industry–education 
integration model, some limitations remain. Firstly, sample size constraints represent an important limitation 
of this study. The study involved 300 students, which, although providing statistical confidence, is a relatively 
small sample size that may limit the generalizability and extrapolation of the findings. Future studies could 
consider expanding the sample size to cover a wider range of students and diverse educational backgrounds, 
thereby enhancing the universality and reliability of the results. Secondly, the time frame of data collection 
limited the ability to assess the long-term effects of the model. With a data collection period of one year, this 
study restricted the evaluation of the long-term impact of the proposed model. Longitudinal data tracking could 
provide deeper insights into the lasting effects of the BPNN-based industry–education integration model on 
student development, including career progression and lifelong learning. Thus, future research could extend the 
data collection period to assess the long-term effects and impact of the model.

Conclusion
Research contribution
This study introduces a BPNN-based industry–education integration model, offering innovative approaches for 
enhancing the educational quality in application-oriented universities. The main contributions are as follows: 
At the theoretical level, this study systematically examines the application of BPNN in industry–education 
integration, addressing an existing gap in the field. Practically, the study demonstrates that this model significantly 
enhances students’ overall competencies and employability. This improvement is reflected in measurable gains in 
academic performance, hands-on skills, innovation, employment rates, job satisfaction, career planning abilities, 
and overall user satisfaction. On the policy front, this model provides valuable insights for educational leaders 
and decision-makers, supporting initiatives that incorporate advanced technologies to improve educational 
quality. By aligning with the increasing demand from society and industry for highly skilled, application-
oriented professionals, this study not only enriches the theoretical framework of industry–education integration 
but also presents concrete, actionable strategies for elevating teaching standards in applied universities.
Future works and research limitations
Although this study has achieved significant results, some challenges and limitations remain. Firstly, the sample 
size is limited, which may affect the generalizability and reliability of the findings. Expanding the sample in 
future research would provide a broader understanding of the model’s effectiveness across different populations 
and contexts. Secondly, the data collection period was relatively short, which restricts the ability to assess the 
long-term effects of the model. Extending the experimental period would allow for a more thorough evaluation 
of its sustained impact on student outcomes. Additionally, the model’s generalization ability requires further 
verification, and future studies could explore data from more dimensions and diverse application scenarios 
to assess its robustness and adaptability. Future research directions include: (1) Deepening multimodal data 
fusion by incorporating text, images, videos, and other data sources, which would improve the model’s overall
